planting.note: Start indoors under warm conditions and transplant only once nights stay reliably above 50F; this cultivar's advantage over standard Genovese basil is disease resistance, not frost hardiness.

directions: Sow indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once the weather is reliably warm. Thunderstruck DMR is one of the later Rutgers University sweet-basil releases, bred and selected specifically for vigorous, high-yield production suited to bunching, microgreens, and processing markets rather than just fresh-market leaf sales; it carries the same downy mildew resistance as its Rutgers sibling releases (Devotion, Obsession, Passion) but was bred with faster regrowth and heavier cutting yields in mind. The medium-to-large leaves are slightly ruffled and bright green with the classic sweet, clove-and-anise Genovese aroma. Because it resists Peronospora belbahrii, Thunderstruck DMR keeps producing clean, marketable leaf through the humid conditions that typically shut down conventional Genovese basil for repeated cut-and-regrow harvests.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: Wild Magic Basil (Herbalea Sterile Ornamental-Culinary Basil)

planting.note: This sterile hybrid basil is propagated only from cuttings and is typically purchased as a started plant; set out after all frost danger has passed in full sun.

directions: Plant started cuttings in well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, or grow in containers and overwinter indoors in cold climates. Wild Magic, part of the Herbalea breeding series, is a sterile interspecific basil hybrid that flowers continuously all season with showy magenta-purple bracts and blooms, resembling an ornamental ageratum as much as a culinary herb, while never setting viable seed. Because the flowers never mature to seed, the plant channels its energy into nonstop bloom and fresh leaf production rather than bolting and turning bitter the way seed-grown basils do once they flower. The bright green leaves carry a mild, sweet, faintly Thai-basil-like flavor and can be harvested continuously alongside the edible flower spikes, which make an attractive, mildly spicy garnish. It also tolerates cooler nights better than most seed-grown sweet basils, extending the usable season at both ends.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in full sun; purple color deepens with more sun exposure and cooler night temperatures.

directions: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the danger of frost has passed. Purple Delight produces some of the darkest, most saturated near-black purple leaves of any basil cultivar, holding its intense coloration even in the interior of the plant rather than fading to green-purple like many older purple selections. The taller, more vigorous habit than Dark Opal or Osmin makes it useful both as a dramatic landscape accent and as a productive cutting herb. The flavor is a strong, classic sweet-basil profile with a mild peppery edge, well suited to purple-tinted vinegars, infused oils, and garnish where maximum color saturation is the goal. Pinch flower spikes regularly to prolong leaf production and prevent the plant from bolting in peak summer heat.
sources: Trade Winds Fruit — Ocimum basilicum seed variety documentation

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in full sun to partial shade; this rare basil is slower and less vigorous to establish than common sweet basil and benefits from consistently warm soil.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; New Guinea Basil is an uncommon, small-statured basil type with narrow, arrow-shaped leaves only about 1.5-2 in long, dark green on top with a distinct dark-purple wash and purple leaf veins and undersides, topped by showy violet flower spikes. Its fragrance is unusual among basils — a strong, sweet licorice scent layered with mint and spice notes rather than the clove-anise character typical of Genovese or Thai basil. Because of its compact size, colorful foliage, and striking flowers, it is grown as much for its ornamental value in pots and border edges as for culinary use, though the aromatic leaves can be used sparingly wherever a licorice-mint basil note is wanted. It performs best as a container or edging plant rather than a large cutting-production basil.
sources: Trade Winds Fruit — Ocimum basilicum New Guinea seed documentation

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; contain with a buried barrier or grow in a pot, as this mint spreads by rhizome like other mints.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Egyptian Mint is a large, vigorous mint with soft, rounded, gray-green woolly leaves closely related to apple mint but taller and more robust, reaching up to 3 ft with spikes of pale lavender flowers in late summer. Its flavor is notably milder and sweeter than spearmint or peppermint, with none of the sharp menthol bite of Mentha x piperita cultivars, making it the traditional mint of choice in Middle Eastern cooking for tabbouleh, yogurt sauces, and mint tea where a subtle, gentle mint note is preferred over an assertive one. The soft, fuzzy leaf texture and pale green-gray color also distinguish it visually from smoother-leaved spearmint types already in cultivation. Harvest leaves regularly through the season; the plant tolerates heat well for a mint and holds flavor even in warm weather.
sources: Mountain Valley Growers — Mentha niliaca variety documentation

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; contain in a pot or buried barrier to limit rhizome spread, as with all mints.

directions: Plant rooted divisions in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, containing the spreading rhizomes in a pot or buried barrier. Japanese Mint is the specific menthol-type variety of corn mint that has been selected and cultivated for centuries in Japan, China, and India for industrial menthol crystal production, carrying a substantially higher menthol content in its essential oil than the wild Mentha arvensis species. The rounded, bright green leaves have an intensely strong, almost sharp peppermint aroma and flavor, more concentrated and cooling than either spearmint or standard peppermint, so it is best used sparingly for tea and flavoring rather than as a general cooking herb. Its dense clusters of small pale-purple flowers form tight whorls at the leaf axils in summer. Harvest and dry stems for menthol-rich tea or extraction; cutting the plant back hard before flowering maximizes both leaf yield and menthol concentration.
